subject: physics

items.q: Which statement about the molecules of a gas is correct?
items.correct: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to their average kinetic energy.
items.misconception: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is set by their total kinetic energy.
items.why: Students know a large hot object stores more energy than a small one at the same temperature, and conclude that temperature must measure the total. The word 'average' is easy to drop when reciting the statement. Two containers of the same gas at the same temperature have the same average molecular kinetic energy even if one holds ten times as many molecules and therefore ten times the total energy. Temperature tracks the average, not the total.
items.random_wrong: They all move at one single fixed speed, and the temperature of the gas is set by that shared speed.

items.q: A sealed container of gas is heated and the temperature of the gas rises. What happens to the molecules of the gas?
items.correct: Their average kinetic energy rises, so the molecules move faster on average.
items.misconception: They all speed up by exactly the same amount and keep sharing one common speed.
items.why: Textbook animations show identical particles bouncing about identically, so 'random' is read as random direction only. The single value implied by 'the temperature' encourages a single value for speed too. The motion is random in both speed and direction. Collisions constantly redistribute energy, so at any instant some molecules are fast and some are slow. Only the average kinetic energy is fixed by the temperature.
items.random_wrong: Each molecule expands, so the gas now fills more of the container space.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume cannot change. The gas is then heated. What happens to the pressure the gas exerts?
items.correct: It increases, because the molecules hit the walls harder.
items.misconception: It stays the same, because the trapped gas is not able to expand.
items.why: Students link pressure changes to volume changes only. If nothing can move, they conclude that nothing can change, forgetting that the molecular motion has changed. Pressure depends on how the molecules move, not only on the space available. Heating raises their average kinetic energy, so collisions with the fixed walls become more frequent and more forceful and the pressure rises.
items.random_wrong: It falls, because the heated molecules swell and spread apart.

items.q: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?
items.correct: The molecules of the gas colliding with the walls of it.
items.misconception: The gas molecules repelling each other and pushing on the walls.
items.why: Students who have met electrostatic repulsion look for a force acting between particles at a distance, and 'a gas fills its container' sounds like something is pushing the particles apart. Gas molecules exert almost no force on each other except during the brief moments they collide. Pressure comes from the impacts themselves — countless collisions each second, each giving the wall a tiny push.
items.random_wrong: The weight of the gas above pressing down on the container.

items.q: Two identical rigid sealed flasks hold the same gas. Flask X is kept at 20 °C and flask Y at 80 °C. Why is the pressure in flask Y higher?
items.correct: The molecules in Y have a greater average kinetic energy, so they hit the walls harder.
items.misconception: The molecules in Y have swollen to a larger size, so they press harder on the walls.
items.why: Students meet thermal expansion of solids and liquids first and carry 'heating makes things bigger' down to the particle scale. Diagrams that draw hot gas particles as larger circles reinforce it. Heating changes how fast the molecules move, not how big they are. The size of a molecule does not change with temperature. It is the greater average kinetic energy — faster molecules, more frequent and harder collisions — that raises the pressure.
items.random_wrong: The molecules in Y repel one another far more strongly at the higher temperature.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas is cooled while its volume is kept constant. Using the particle model, what happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.correct: It decreases, because slower molecules hit the walls less often and less hard.
items.misconception: It stays the same, because the rigid container will not let the gas shrink at all.
items.why: Students link pressure changes to volume changes only. If nothing can move, they conclude that nothing can change, forgetting that the molecular motion has changed. Pressure depends on how the molecules move, not only on the space available. Heating raises their average kinetic energy, so collisions with the fixed walls become more frequent and more forceful and the pressure rises.
items.random_wrong: It increases, because the cooled molecules move closer to the walls of it.

items.q: The pressure of a gas produces a net force on the wall of its container. In which direction does that net force act?
items.correct: At right angles to the surface of the container wall.
items.misconception: At an angle that depends on the shape of the container.
items.why: Students picture a stream of gas blowing past a surface, as in a wind, and transfer that sideways push to a sealed container. Arrows drawn tangentially on diagrams of curved vessels reinforce it. In a sealed gas the molecules arrive from all directions, so the components of their impacts along the wall cancel. Only the perpendicular components survive, giving a net force at right angles to the wall whatever the shape of the container.
items.random_wrong: Along the surface of the wall, in the direction of flow.

items.q: Which statement about a gas and changes of pressure is correct?
items.correct: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes.
items.misconception: A gas keeps a fixed volume whatever pressure is applied to it.
items.why: The rule learned for liquids — takes the shape of its container, keeps a fixed volume — is over-applied to gases, since both are fluids and are taught together. A liquid keeps a fixed volume, but a gas does not. Its molecules are far apart, so raising the pressure squeezes them into a smaller volume and lowering the pressure lets the gas expand.
items.random_wrong: A gas can be expanded by pressure changes but never compressed.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas is allowed to expand into a larger volume at constant temperature. Using the particle model, why does the pressure decrease?
items.correct: The molecules travel further between wall collisions, so there are fewer collisions.
items.misconception: Each molecule strikes the wall more gently, since it now has less kinetic energy.
items.why: Students associate 'spread out' with 'weaker' and assume that having more space costs the molecules energy. Constant temperature is stated but is not connected to constant average speed. At constant temperature the average kinetic energy — and so the force of a typical impact — is unchanged. What changes is the rate of collisions: a bigger space means longer journeys between hits, so the pressure falls.
items.random_wrong: The molecules cool down as they spread out into the much larger space.

items.q: Under which conditions does the relationship pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas?
items.correct: A fixed mass of gas that is being held at a constant temperature.
items.misconception: Any mass of gas at all, whatever its temperature happens to be doing.
items.why: The relationship is memorised as a formula without its conditions, and those conditions appear in the line above the equation rather than in the equation itself. The conditions are part of the statement: a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature. Heat the gas, or let some of it escape, and the product p V changes value.
items.random_wrong: A fixed mass of gas whose temperature is steadily climbing.

items.q: For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, which relationship does the specification give?
items.correct: pressure × volume = constant, written as [p V = constant]
items.misconception: pressure ÷ volume = constant, written as [p / V = a constant]
items.why: Most GCSE relationships met before this one are direct proportions, so students default to 'one up, the other up'. The word 'constant' is read as describing the pair rather than their product. It is the product p V that stays constant, not the ratio. If the pressure doubles the volume must halve to keep the product the same, so pressure and volume always move in opposite directions.
items.random_wrong: pressure + volume = constant, written as [p + V = constant]

items.q: Which units does the specification give for the two quantities in p V = constant?
items.correct: Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres cubed, m^3.
items.misconception: Pressure in newtons, N, and volume in centimetres cubed, cm^3.
items.why: Pressure and force are used interchangeably in everyday speech, and pressure is introduced through the force a gas exerts, so the force unit is the one students reach for. Pressure is force spread over an area, so its unit is not the force unit. The specification gives pressure, p, in pascals, Pa; one pascal is one newton per square metre.
items.random_wrong: Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in cubic centimetres, cm^3.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 0.125 m^3 at a pressure of 80 kPa. At constant temperature the pressure is increased to 800 kPa. What is the new volume of the gas?
items.why: The relationship is memorised as a formula without its conditions, and those conditions appear in the line above the equation rather than in the equation itself. The conditions are part of the statement: a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature. Heat the gas, or let some of it escape, and the product p V changes value.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas at a pressure of 300 kPa occupies 0.020 m^3. At constant temperature it is allowed to expand to 0.150 m^3. What is the new pressure of the gas?
items.correct: 40 kPa
items.misconception: 300 kPa
items.why: The relationship is memorised as a formula without its conditions, and those conditions appear in the line above the equation rather than in the equation itself. The conditions are part of the statement: a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature. Heat the gas, or let some of it escape, and the product p V changes value.

items.q: In physics, what is meant by work?
items.correct: Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
items.misconception: Work is the energy stored inside a moving body.
items.why: The calculation W = F s is met before the definition, so students describe work by its formula. Others confuse work, the transfer, with the kinetic energy store it may fill. Work names the process of transferring energy, not a force and not a store. A force does work when it moves something, and the energy transferred in that process is the work done.
items.random_wrong: Work is a force acting over a given distance.

items.q: A cyclist uses a bicycle pump to inflate a tyre, and the barrel of the pump becomes noticeably warm. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Work is done on the gas as it is compressed, raising its internal energy.
items.misconception: Friction between the piston seal and the barrel is the only cause of the warming.
items.why: Friction is the standard explanation for anything that gets warm when it is rubbed or moved, and students can feel the piston sticking, so a familiar cause displaces the unfamiliar one. Friction contributes a little, but the main effect is that the piston does work on the gas as it compresses it. That transfer increases the internal energy of the gas, so its temperature rises and the barrel warms.
items.random_wrong: Warm air is drawn in from outside, and that air heats the metal barrel.

items.q: Does gas pressure in a sealed container act downwards, like weight?
items.correct: No. It acts at right angles to every surface the gas touches, including the lid of the container.
items.misconception: Gas pressure acts downwards, because the weight of the gas presses on the surface below it.
items.why: Pressure is often introduced with a block resting on a table, where the force really is the weight acting downwards. Students transfer that single-direction picture to gases. Gas pressure comes from molecular collisions, and these happen on the base, the sides and the lid of a container alike. The weight of the gas is negligible compared with the force from those collisions.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A volume is quoted in cubic centimetres. Can it be used directly in p V = constant?
items.correct: Not as it stands — the specification gives volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.
items.misconception: Any volume unit will do, because the units cancel when the two states are compared.
items.why: In p1 V1 = p2 V2 the units genuinely do cancel if both volumes use the same unit, so students generalise to cases where they do not, and mix cm^3 with m^3 in one calculation. Both volumes must be in the same unit, and the specification's unit is metres cubed. Convert every volume to m^3 first — mixing cm^3 and m^3 in one calculation gives an answer wrong by a factor of a million.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A gas sealed in a pump is compressed quickly and its temperature rises. Where did the energy come from?
items.correct: From the person pushing the piston, who does work on the gas.
items.misconception: From warm air drawn in from the surroundings, or from the warmth of the cyclist's hands.
items.why: Students expect temperature rises to come from heating by a hotter object, because every earlier example of a temperature rise involved a heat source. No hotter object is needed. Energy is transferred mechanically: the force on the piston moves through a distance, doing work on the gas and increasing its internal energy, which raises its temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What unit is used for the volume V in p V = constant?
items.correct: Metres cubed, m^3.
items.misconception: Metres squared, m^2, the unit that appears in the definition of pressure.
items.why: Because pressure involves an area in m^2, students carry the squared unit across to the other quantity in the same equation, and 'cubed' and 'squared' are easily swapped under exam pressure. Volume fills space in three dimensions, so its unit is metres cubed, m^3. The specification states volume, V, in metres cubed; m^2 is an area, not a volume.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A gas is compressed and work is done on it. What happens to its internal energy?
items.correct: The internal energy of the gas increases.
items.misconception: The internal energy falls, because squeezing the gas forces energy out of it.
items.why: Students picture squeezing a sponge, where squeezing pushes something out, and they also confuse internal energy with the volume the gas occupies. Doing work on a gas transfers energy into it, so the internal energy increases and the temperature can rise. Nothing is squeezed out of a sealed gas — the same molecules simply store more energy.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A gas at 300 kPa in 0.020 m^3 expands to 0.150 m^3 at constant temperature. How is the new pressure found?
items.correct: Multiply 300 kPa by 0.020 m^3 and divide by 0.150 m^3, which gives a smaller pressure.
items.misconception: Multiply 300 kPa by 0.150 m^3 and divide by 0.020 m^3, which gives a larger pressure.
items.why: Students substitute the numbers into a remembered ratio without asking which way the answer should go, so the volume ratio ends up inverted. Check the direction first: the gas has expanded, so the pressure must fall. Only p1 V1 ÷ V2 gives a smaller pressure; if the answer is bigger than the starting pressure, the ratio has been inverted.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
